utterances.text: Yes. This is the end of the war. There were some more incidents after that, but this was the end of the Croatian-Muslim war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have examined the dates of deaths, but on the 16th -- but I haven't come across the date the 16th of April. Is it possible that not a single member of the HVO was killed on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this list is not absolutely accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly not, because on the 16th of April, members of other units from Vitez municipality may have been killed, people who are not from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have studied this document. I have an advantage over Mrs. Glumac because I had more time to study it. I'm just saying, to avoid the debate taking an undesirable course, regarding the 16th of April there are names 333, 319 and 380, and two of them are said to have died at Stari Vitez and the third at Poculica. So that was the question of the Defence, "Were any victims in Ahmici recorded on the 16th of April?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you give me the numbers once again? I'm not sure I got them right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. 363, Kristo Stipo Anto and the date given is the 16th of April, 1993 in Poculica. 379, a bit lower down, and 380, two persons who died, again on the 16th of April, in Stari Vitez. I may have forgotten others, but these are the only ones I've found for this date the 16th of April, and may counsel correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I thank the Prosecutor counsel for this additional explanation. Yes, these are some things that -- these are numbers that I didn't notice in the text, and it is very useful for me to know this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dragica Prkacin, born in 1934, she figure under the number 380. Was she a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is obvious that the lady was 59 years old at the time. It is a poor family. Her son Vlado was a handicapped person in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Her son Vlado is the person figuring under 379, Prkacin Vlado, mother's name Dragica, born in 1955; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And he was disabled?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was in a wheelchair. His body was found, and his mother's body, in spite of many attempts by her other son, who was alive, never found the body. The hut they lived in was set on fire, and it is assumed that her body burned together with the house, the hut.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was that hut in the area of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The hut was in a part of Stari Vitez known as Mahala and which was under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The forces of the BH army remained in that part of the town that is in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You have given us some additional information now. Is the exact date of his death known, or is it just assumed that it happened in the first days of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is assumed that it was on the 16th, but it could have easily been the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I don't think the Prosecutor has denied what I am saying. There is only one name that I am not sure that he was a soldier or not. In Poculica, as far as I know, the Vitez Brigade was not there at all on the 16th of April, and then these other two are civilians. So we have no further information about any person who was killed on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Anto Kristo from Poculica was also a civilian, and also from the year of his birth we can see that he was over 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So according to you, is this list correct, as regards the date of the demise of the persons listed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This list in principle can be said to carry the correct dates, but, as I have already emphasised, in view of the situation that prevailed at the time these documents were made, it was impossible to claim emphatically that each of these dates was correct. However, there can't be major differences, and most of this data can be treated as being credible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the cross-examination, you said that the persons that disappeared at Kuber did not disappear on the 18th, that went missing. We also come across information that these were not HVO members but civilians, so that is why I am asking you how valuable this list is, how correct is the information in these lists for us to be able to rely on them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I claim categorically that maybe several dozen names are missing from this list because there were many displaced persons in Vitez, and one can come across names of Muslim inhabitants here, but in principle, this data in most cases, in my judgment, is correct, because in the first few days, the number of dead was not so high that they couldn't be registered. Later on, these numbers increased daily, and then the possibility of error increased too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please look at the last page, page number 10. There is a group of children there, born in '85, '83, '75. These are numbers 512, 513, 514, 519, 520, 523, 524, 525. These are children. Were these children HVO members?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This tragedy or misfortune occurred on the 10th of June, 1993, and to my great misfortune, ten days after the shell fell and hit children playing, I was on the spot because it is only some 300 or 350 metres away from our command, a camera arrived very quickly, and this camera, video camera, recorded the most terrible pictures that I have ever seen in my life. Unfortunately, I saw this with my own eyes. And I saw mothers collecting pieces of the bodies of their children, and some body parts were, in fact, hanging on the surrounding trees. This is a picture and a videotape that TV stations based in Bila, where the British battalion was based, would not accept. The journalists literally told us that they cannot broadcast such images to their citizens, and that that was the only reason why they did not wish to take this videotape from us and broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did this shell fall? I am asking you whether it was close to the frontline or was it in the civilian part of Vitez where only citizens were at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The shell fell in a suburb called Kamenjace, and apart from civilian homes, within a radius of 400 metres, there can be no military targets, no soldiers, no facilities of any kind except family homes and gardens and a small improvised playground with a basket for basketball where the children were, in fact, playing basketball.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: My question, in fact, was whether the children who were killed were members of the HVO because of the heading that this list carries?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is written by hand here that a certain number of civilians were included, and judging by the dates of birth of these children, it is obvious. The oldest among them was 10 or 12. I can't see it now here on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So obviously this is not a list of HVO members killed, but included are a large number of civilians as well; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You spoke about your relationship with Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic, Midhat Varupa, and some other inhabitants of Vitez who left that area. Some of them were killed in the conflict. Tell me, what was your attitude towards Muslims, very briefly, and in those days, particularly at the beginning of the conflict, did you assist anyone and how and what your reaction was to this situation in general?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It may be embarrassing for me to speak about some of the humane gestures I made, but at your request, I will tell you. Of course, I assisted, I would say many people. I would even say that, fortunately, I was not the only good man around, to put it in those words. At the beginning of that conflict, I think one can talk of hundreds of Croats who, in that situation, assisted the Muslims because they were in a position to do so. In my house, in my apartment, which is literally on the line of separation, throughout the war, we didn't have a single window frame, the furniture was riddled with dozens of sniper bullets and other bullets and shrapnel. It was inhabited by my wife and my daughter who was under age. But our neighbour two floors above us, a Muslim, would spend several nights there because she felt safer with my wife because for her the fact that my wife's husband was a member of the HVO meant security. In the most critical days, at the beginning, this Muslim woman's two sons, I can give you the surname of that family, Jelaskovic, they were the same age as my daughters. They grew up with my daughters and went to the same schools as my daughters. And my wife hid both of them when it was critical, one in a cupboard and the other one in the bed. She tied a scarf around his head. Because he still wasn't shaving, he could get away with pretending to be a girl. And when the worst was over some ten or fifteen days later, they crossed over into Muslim territory. They are alive and well, and they often call us up, me and my daughters and wife. There are other examples. I would take medicines to the detainees in the cinema and even cigarettes to one of them who was not a friend even. He asked me to try and provide his wife and children with food because they had nothing in the apartment and in their own house, they had a house and an apartment, there was plenty of food. So with the official driver of the brigade and the wife of this Muslim, his surname is Seaganovic, his nickname Zeko, I don't know his first name because he was not a close friend, we went to his house and took flour, oil, and sugar to his apartment. And I emphasise, I do not wish to boast, but there were tens and hundreds of such examples of human beings helping other human beings, even in those very difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You just mentioned a woman whose sons hid in your house on the 16th and who stayed on in hiding in your apartment. What was her name?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Her name is Zumra Jelaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were answering questions by the Prosecutor about Muhamed Mujezinovic. Do you know whether Mario Cerkez gave guarantees to Muhamed Mujezinovic and his family after his release from the cinema, that they were given assurances or guarantees that they would not be attacked?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The security of the brigade, security officers of the brigade, escorted Muhamed home, and a number of soldiers were tasked to supervise Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic's home around the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The statement that was shown to you by the Prosecutor and which alleges that a cessation of hostilities was required and another attempt to be made at coexistence was signed, on the one hand, by Ivica Santic as president of the HVO government and, on the other, by Muhamed Mujezinovic. What was Muhamed Mujezinovic at the time? You spoke about this in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic was president of the war presidency in the part of Vitez under the control of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you have many more questions on this issue, because we should now take a 15-minute break? Is it convenient for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is convenient. I won't have many more, but I do have some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: A 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, just several more questions regarding the situation on the 16th, considering that the Prosecutor asked you whether you knew what was happening in Ahmici. Did you have information about what was going on in other places? In other words, what other locations were places of conflict on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It may sound strange, but I really had more information from other locations in the Vitez municipality. The war really engulfed the whole area, as I stated to the Prosecutor, and the conflicts raged at the area of Brdo. This is a feature that dominates the Lasva Valley. In the village of Poculica the Muslim army had attacked --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Excuse me just one moment. Could we get the Exhibit number 1, which is the large map of the Lasva River Valley, so that this witness could point to the places where the most intense fighting happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, would you show to the Trial Chamber the locations where the most intense conflicts raged on 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether this map was put together correctly, but let me try to orient myself here. This is the road leading to Travnik. From Vitez in that direction of Travnik. In this area of the Vitez municipality there were no conflicts, that is the area of Nova Bila. The area of Veliki, and Mali Mosunj, and then the area of Zabilje. However, somewhere between Zabilje and Sadovaca, that is where this feature is called Brdo, which dominates the entire area of the Lasva Valley. Sadovaca is a village which is completely Muslim, whereas Zabilje is 100 per cent Croatian, and Bila is predominantly Croatian and had a small percentage of Muslims, whereas Veliki and Mali were greater and lesser -- are predominantly Croatian. These areas here are Croatian, and from Sadovaca there is the village of Bukve and Preocica. These defence lines of Jardol and Krcevine were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what is the ethnic composition of Preocica?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Preocica is the largest local commune in the Vitez municipality and over 90 per cent is Muslim, with the exception of a small hamlet which before the war was populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what was the population size so that we can assess the size of this village?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Preocica number over 3.000 inhabitants, and with the refugees who were arriving, some estimates put the number at 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there -- on the 16th of April, did the Croatian side conduct any war operations towards Preocica?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Preocica is relatively far from the defence lines and from Croatian villages, and it's much more elevated. So it's much higher than where the positions of the Croatian troops were. To my knowledge, there were no operations in that direction, because for that you needed guns and mortar support. You needed 120-millimetre guns. As far as I know, there were no operations conducted towards Preocica on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What other places were caught up in fighting?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Around here there is a road going to Zenica, and this is the village of Poculica, which is also strategically important, in my view. And obviously in the assessment view of the Bosnian army it is very important because it is on the Veternica pass and it borders the Zenica municipality. Later on, from this position, there was fire opened from tank towards Vitez. This area is predominantly populated by Croats, and in one area towards Prnjavor, this was populated by Muslims. Croatian population from this area did not have a connection, that is the physical connection. In other words, Croat houses were not -- and their properties were not contiguous. In other words, they were an enclave surrounded by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what happened in Poculica on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Early in the morning but we only learned about this in the evening of the 16th, the Muslim army took all civilians prisoner and locked them up in some houses, some barns and a little social club that they had. Since we were on -- occupying a dominant feature, we saw a number of plumes of smoke and houses on fire. Later on we learned that a couple of Muslim soldiers, either inebriated or maybe for some other reason, came to a room where 30 or 40 Croats were kept locked and shot through the door. As far as I know, about four people died there and another seven or eight were injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you saw houses on fire in Poculica. Whose houses were they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were Croat houses, and they still stand as a monument of the savagery at that time because no Croat has ever gone back since.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where else was there fighting on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are the areas which are purely Muslim. This is a Muslim village, a fairly large village, and Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic, I may mention, was born there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What village is this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's called Vrhovine, and it is immediately above the location where that crime took place. It dominates Ahmici, Pirici and Santici and the road leading to Busovaca from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is the ethnic composition of Vrhovine and was there any fighting there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vrhovine are exclusively Muslim, and on these first days there were no combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mean on the part of Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct, on the part of Croats, because here too you could only conduct any combat operations with artillery support.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you now point to Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sivrino Selo is here. It is located between the road connecting Vitez and Busovaca and the road leading from Vitez to Zenica. And here is a road connecting -- alongside the road there were some Croatian houses, which in the first days of war, 16th and 17th, were all burnt down and its inhabitants were driven into the Vitez town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the HVO conduct any operations towards Sivrino Selo on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 16th there was no combat operations of the HVO to the north of Vitez, except that there were fierce fighting and defence around Jardol and Krcevine, because the Muslim forces attacked from this direction, probably believing that this would be the best place to break through the defence lines and emerge on the road leading to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How about Kruscica? Where is Kruscica located and what is its ethnic composition? Their Honours will not be able to see if you step over that way.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kruscica is one of the largest local communes in the Vitez municipality. It is this area here, and it was very developed in the times of Austro-Hungary because it is rich in woods. And this village was urbanised. It had two motels and a hotel, it had its own source of water. It was predominantly Muslim, especially the part closer to the wood, whereas this area closer to the town was populated more by Croats. And this is actually where also the only municipal cemetery, the Catholic cemetery, was located. On the first day, the few Croats that were there were in the part predominantly inhabited by Muslims were driven out, a few of them fled. One could flee through these woods here towards the town. Throughout the day there were -- there was fighting between Croatian units in the area of Rijeka, closer to the town, and so the fighting was -- the attack came towards the area populated by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Kruscica remain in Muslim hands until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It remained in the Muslim hands until the end of the war, and what I also want to point out is that the original waterworks installation are located, which provide much of the water supply to the town of Vitez, which is why most -- most citizens of the town of Vitez were without water for the most part of the war. The water would be cut off, and then under the pressure of the International Community would be again given, and then we had a similar problem with the power as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But on the 16th all Croats had left Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Except for those who were unaccounted for, those who were detained, and as I said, some just fled through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How about Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The village of Gacice is very close to the town centre, and it is populated -- I'm not sure -- I believe it's about 50 per cent Croats and 50 per cent Muslims. In the first three or four days there was no shooting or no -- there was no violence there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Donja Veceriska also had a mixed population, and in the beginning there was fierce fighting. There were some Muslims houses set on fire but also some Croat houses set on fire. One part of the village was occupied by the Muslims and the other by Croats. There was separation there, there was some violence on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the strategic position of Donja Veceriska with respect to Vitezit and the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it clearly. Donja Veceriska is above the large Vitezit factory compound. It is maybe -- its elevation is about 50 metres above that of the factory. This is where the SPS facilities are. And from Donja Veceriska you can throw a rock, as our people would say, on the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So there was fierce fighting there. How about Stari Vitez, the Old Vitez? In fact, Mahala.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the town centre. This is the soccer field, which during the war was the line of separation. Croats were on this side of the stadium and Muslims on this side. There was a row of garages here which were in a neutral zone, and just beyond the garages is the house where I lived and which I occupied before the war, during the war and still occupy today. This is the part of Old Vitez which is called Mahala. There are no strict limits of it, people just call it Stari Vitez or Old Vitez. Some call it Mahala. I believe that the correct way is to call it Stari Vitez and then part of it is maybe Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the 16th there was fierce fighting there, and did Stari Vitez remain under the BH army control until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the first day there was fierce fighting there, and I believe that you could infer from my own statement that there were constantly problems over Mahala and the Muslim efforts to create a bastion there. They kept digging trenches there, whereas the Croats asked, "Why are you digging trenches towards the town?" But this was a problem that was with us constantly. About 15 or 20 Croat families lived there, and a few of them stayed there throughout the war. One of them -- a part fled and a part was exchanged. Some people fared relatively well, so to speak, because they were protected by the Muslims, part of them very badly because nobody protected them, and there were casualties. A member of the HVO lived in Mahala with his young wife. He was renting a place there. We learned that several days into the fighting, his throat was cut, literally. I believe his name was Miskovic, I'm not certain, but his wife still lives there, and this information can easily be verified. Another one had bad luck, that he was with his girlfriend when the conflict started and was captured, obviously, by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only have two more questions. Could you please sit down again now? In cross-examination, the Prosecutor showed you a document which stated that the situation was calm in Zenica on the 16th. What was your information about the state of things on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm glad that I can comment on that document. I do not question the fact that there was calm between the 15th and the 16th, but what type of calm was there? I also told you that it was quiet in Zenica when I visited there, that there were MUP forces and military. But what was the reason? And I don't know what motivated the gentleman who drafted that document. I told you honestly what I experienced in Zenica. However, some other reports speak differently. They would say that the 16th was not quiet, at least not quiet for Croats. In the afternoon and in the evening, some Croats managed to get across from Zenica, and we learned what happened in Zenica on that day. What was going on was arrest of the HVO members in their homes, in the streets, there were raids; and on these initial days of the conflict in the Lasva Valley, there were some places which became notorious for Croats: the music school and other places, they were filled with HVO members, and then with Croats from other areas in Zenica, which speaks to the fact that over 10.000 Croats were driven from Zenica. Zenica was one of the large centres, Croatian centres, in Central Bosnia, not in terms of percentage but in terms of the concentration of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is the distance between Vitez and Zenica, across the Vjetrenice pass?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Using the road which I mentioned and which I used the day before the conflict, that is, from the intersection, not from the centre of Vitez town, so from the highway to Busovaca, from that intersection to the first suburbs of Zenica, it is 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croats were detained in Zenica on those initial days and detained in the music school and the correctional centre?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I think it is between 2.000 and 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Another piece of information which you provided concerning the village of Stranjani, which is near Zenica, and you mentioned the ethnic cleansing had started as early as the 16th and that people from that area, which is a village, really, it is a suburb but more like villages adjoining Zenica, that people started arriving there as early as the 16th.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Not just from Stranjani but Cajdras and some other villages which I now cannot now recall, but those were the villages which were ethnically mostly purely Croatian and were on the south side and were facing the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One more thing. The Croats who were detained in Zenica, that is, the HVO members and civilians, were they exchanged and when?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This issue further complicated the relations between the Croats and Muslims, which was complicated enough, because the agreement on the exchange which was mediated through the BRITBAT and the UNHCR was not respected by the military authorities in Zenica and they did not release Croat detainees. They only did so later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The persons mentioned by Dr. Mujezinovic in the Blaskic case also includes Ivan Santic and Pero Skopljak. Do you know what happened to them since they had been accused of committing war crimes and one of the charges was based on this statement by Dr. Mujezinovic concerning the incidents which you also testified to. Can you say, were they released?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were detained here, but justice prevailed like always and they came back home after about 70 days of detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One additional question. I believe there may have been an error in the transcript. Did members of HOS ever become members of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they never did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which unit did they become members of, which special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They all became members of the Vitezovi special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Cilic, I thank you. This concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see counsel Susak. Are you going to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is a matter I want to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. We rule that only counsel who examined the witness in chief is allowed to re-examine the witness, so that counsel who cross-examined the witness are not allowed to re-examine him. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is just what I wanted to say because I participated in the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no, no. We regard your participation in that examination as cross-examination. This witness was called by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, so she was entitled to examine him in chief, and he was cross-examined by other Defence counsel, then cross-examined by the Prosecution, and so we feel that only Defence counsel, as I said, who examined him in chief is entitled to re-examination. This is our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But may I just say that during the examination-in-chief, I did not have access to all the documents that this witness was examined about today in the cross-examination. But if that is your ruling, of course, I will abide by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, may I put a question linked to this question of re-examination? Of course, we will respect the ruling of the Court, but we feel that this could lead to certain problems; namely, today we saw that the Prosecutor, in the course of his cross-examination, presented some documents for the first time and mentioned a particular accused by name. By such a ruling, we are unable to refer back to that document or that exhibit, and the Prosecutor, on the other hand, will be given the chance to present certain evidence which we will not be able to comment on. We feel that the principle of equality of arms is thereby impaired. Secondly, we have some common witnesses with other Defence counsel, and in the interests of the efficiency of the proceedings, we have agreed that each one of us should not call witnesses as his own witness but that, within the framework of the examination-in-chief of one witness, one Defence counsel examine him and then another Defence counsel cross-examine him. As a result of this ruling, we would be prevented from re-examining. Therefore, it is my submission that strict observation of this rule would put us in an unequal position. So I am asking Your Honours whether it would be possible for the future, in cases when the Prosecutor, in the cross-examination, mentions any one of the accused, that in those situations, the Defence counsel of that accused be permitted to re-examine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, the motion is not granted. We stick to our ruling concerning re-examination. However, we request the Prosecutor, whenever he decides to disclose new documents, to use new documents in court, to disclose them in advance. As soon as you know the list of witnesses for the following week, if you have any document that you intend to use in court, you should disclose them to the Defence counsel, so roughly a week, I mean, a few days before the relevant witness is called, so that all Defence counsel are in a position to prepare, and in particular, the Defence counsel who is going to examine the witness in chief. All right. So for the time being, we are through with -- yes, Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Of course, we also will abide by your ruling, only there is the question of delay. I cannot accept that this be treated very strictly because on the eve or a day before, a day or two before, we may discover a document that we intend to use. So what I would suggest is that we be obliged to disclose before the testimony of the witness but not necessarily so many days before; and even during the examination-in-chief, it may appear that certain documents are necessary for the cross-examination. If we are required to respect a very strict period in advance, it will be very difficult for us. But I would suggest that we do disclose -- in any case before referring to those documents in court, that we disclose those documents to all the attorneys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let us say as early as possible. If possible, a week in advance, but in any event, before the examination-in-chief, and in such a way to allow the Defence to review and study the document well and prepare for the defence. So good faith is required. Therefore, as soon as possible, as early as possible. If you have a document at the last minute -- because after the examination-in-chief, you suddenly come across a document or one that you may have forgotten -- then we will have to give a period of time to the Defence. Then you will tell us that you have a document that you intend to produce, and in that case, we can postpone the testimony of the witness or find another practical solution to allow the Defence to prepare well on the basis of that document. Are we agreed? Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course I will fully observe your ruling, but in this particular case, I really do think it is an exception, and in my opinion, for justice to be served and in the interest of fairness, I, in this case, should be allowed to re-examine this witness in view of the documents that were presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. We have already made a ruling. I don't see why you in particular should then re-examine him and not the other Defence counsel. Then all of them would be entitled, the ones who were prepared to cross-examine him after the examination-in-chief. The ruling stands, and for the future, we will see to it that the Prosecutor complies with the other ruling concerning his duty to produce documents in advance. The Court has no questions for the witness. Mr. Cilic, thank you so much indeed for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have a few minutes left to discuss future sittings. Counsel Radovic asked that we not sit on this case in the last week of February. Now, let me say that we intend now to go on until the 29th of January, for January, so for the next two weeks, starting on the 19th because on the 18th there is a holiday, an official holiday of our Tribunal. Then we will skip the first week of February and resume on the 8th of February until the Friday, it will be one week, from the 8th through to the 12th, and then from the 15th up to the 17th, Wednesday. We must stop on Wednesday, and so we are not sitting on the 18th, 19th, and 22nd. We were wondering whether this would enable you to go back to your country and prepare, fill in your tax returns, because we would like to resume on the 23rd or the 24th of February, so you would have a few days back home where you could probably attend to that particular problem, and then we would resume on the 23rd or 24th, Tuesday or Wednesday, and sit on this case until the 5th of March, 5th of March, and then we must again skip one week, and then we would resume on the 15th of March, up to a few days before Easter. We were very much hoping that we would finish by Easter, but I see that it is impossible. I don't think it is realistic. I wonder whether then, Counsel Radovic, you suggested that we should skip the last week of February. Would you be prepared to accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the legal deadline for submitting tax returns. It doesn't apply just to me but to all of us. So I think we will come to an agreement, depending on our individual considerations, and if we may, we will let you know on our next working day. As far as I am concerned, this would be satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Because, as I said, you would have the 18th, 19th of February and the 22nd, and, really, if need be, also the 23rd. But we would prefer to resume on Tuesday, the 23rd. Could you be so kind as to let us know, maybe on Tuesday, if this is agreeable? One last question. We intend to call as a witness, as a Court witness, the anthropologist or sociologist who wrote a book which was provided to us by the Prosecutor. I'm sorry, I don't remember her name. I think a copy was also given to all Defence counsel, a photocopy, of that book. So we would like to ask her to come to give evidence in court, also because I assume the book is about the particular village, the particular village in question. Could the Prosecution make preparations so that at some point in time, that witness may be called? Now, I wonder whether the -- I hope all the Defence counsel have gone through that book so they are familiar with that. All right. If there are no outstanding matters, we will adjourn now, and we will sit again on Tuesday at 9.00 sharp. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.22 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of January, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
